seo_title: Low Appraisal in Indiana: What to Do | Your Realty Link
meta_desc: A low appraisal in Indiana does not have to end your deal. Here are your options to cover the gap, renegotiate, or challenge it, with Your Realty Link.
h1: What to Do When Your Appraisal Comes In Low
hero_sub: A low appraisal can rattle even a smooth Central Indiana purchase. Here is what the number really means and the calm, data-driven way to handle it as a buyer or seller.
schema_headline: What to Do When Your Appraisal Comes In Low in Indiana
schema_desc: A calm, practical guide to every option when a home appraisal comes in below the contract price in Central Indiana.
intro: You found the home. Your offer in a busy Fishers cul-de-sac beat out three others, the sellers signed, and everything felt settled — until your lender called to say the home appraisal came back below the price you agreed to pay. If your stomach just dropped reading that, take a breath. A low appraisal is one of the most common bumps in a Central Indiana purchase, and it almost never means the deal is dead. It means it is time to negotiate with a clear head and good information. Here is exactly what a low appraisal means and every option you have.
sections: why-appraisals-come-in-low
Why an Appraisal Comes In Below the Contract Price

An appraisal is a licensed appraiser's independent opinion of value, ordered by your lender to protect the money they are lending. The bank will not loan more than the home is worth to them, so the appraised value sets a ceiling on the loan. When that number lands under your contract price, the shortfall becomes yours to solve, not the lender's.

In a fast-moving market, prices can climb quicker than closed sales can catch up. Appraisers lean heavily on recent comparable sales, and in neighborhoods like Irvington, Broad Ripple, or a new-construction pocket of Westfield, a shortage of recent comps or a bidding war that pushed the price past what the paperwork supports can leave the appraisal short. It is not a personal judgment on your taste or the home.

Other times the culprit is condition, an unusual floor plan, or an honest miss. Whatever the reason, the number is a starting point for a conversation, not a final verdict. For a deeper look at what drags a value down, see our guide on what hurts a home appraisal in Indiana.
what-is-appraisal-gap
Understanding the Appraisal Gap

The difference between what you agreed to pay and what the home appraised for is called the appraisal gap. If you agreed to pay more than the appraised value, the gap is the amount your financing simply will not cover on its own.

Why does it matter so much? Your lender bases the loan on the lower of the price or the appraised value. So the gap has to be bridged somehow — with extra cash, a lower price, or a mix of the two — or the terms of the deal have to change. Understanding the size of the gap is the first step before you weigh any option.

Some buyers in competitive situations sign an appraisal gap clause up front, promising to bring additional cash up to a set amount if the appraisal falls short. If you did that, revisit exactly what you committed to before assuming you have room to push back. What you signed shapes everything that follows.
your-options
Your Five Options When the Number Is Low

Once you know the size of the gap, you and your agent weigh five paths. None is automatically the right one — it depends on how badly each side wants the deal, current market conditions, and what your contract allows.

• Bring extra cash: You pay the difference out of pocket at closing, on top of your down payment, so your loan stays within the appraised value.
  • Ask the seller to lower the price: The seller drops the price to the appraised value so no gap remains.
  • Meet in the middle: You cover part of the gap in cash and the seller reduces the price for the rest.
  • Challenge the appraisal: Request a formal review, called a reconsideration of value, with stronger comparable sales or corrected facts.
  • Walk away: If you kept the right contingency, you cancel and recover your earnest money.

In practice, most deals settle with a lower price, a cash contribution, or a blend of both. Sellers rarely want to restart the process, and committed buyers rarely want to lose the home. The right move comes down to leverage — which brings us to your contract.
contingencies-leverage
How Contingencies Decide Who Has Leverage

The single biggest factor in who holds the upper hand is the contingency structure written into your purchase agreement. An appraisal contingency, along with the related financing contingency, gives a financed buyer the right to renegotiate or cancel and recover earnest money if the appraisal comes in low.

If you waived the appraisal contingency — common in heated multiple-offer situations — you have committed to buy at the contract price regardless, which generally means you must cover the gap or risk losing your earnest money. Sellers know this, and it tilts leverage firmly toward them.

If you kept the contingency, the seller faces a real question: negotiate with you, or put the home back on the market and hope the next buyer's appraisal comes in higher, which it often will not, because a new appraiser sees the same comparable sales. That reality is exactly what brings most sellers back to the table.
challenge-appraisal
Challenging a Low Appraisal With Better Data

You cannot simply demand a higher number, but you can request a reconsideration of value, sometimes called a rebuttal. This is a formal ask to the lender and appraiser to review the report using better comparable sales or corrected facts. It works best when you can show something concrete was missed.

This is where a sharp agent earns their keep. Your Realty Link will pull a fresh comparative market analysis and hunt for stronger comps — recent closed sales that are genuinely more similar in size, condition, location, or upgrades — along with any factual errors in the report. Common wins include:

• Better comparables: More recent or more similar closed sales the appraiser overlooked.
  • Corrected square footage: A miscounted room, level, or finished area.
  • Missed finished space: A finished basement or bonus room not credited.
  • Overlooked upgrades: A renovation, new systems, or high-end finishes not accounted for.
how-yrl-helps
How Your Realty Link Renegotiates Calmly

A low appraisal is an emotional moment, and emotion is exactly what you do not want driving a six-figure negotiation. Janet Giles-Schultz, Principal Broker, and the Your Realty Link team have guided buyers and sellers through this on both sides of the closing table across the MIBOR MLS.

Our approach is calm and data-first: read your contract and contingencies, quantify the gap, map the realistic options, and go back to the other side with numbers instead of ultimatums. If you have ever wondered why the appraised value differs from a website's guess, our breakdown of a CMA versus a Zestimate in Indianapolis explains where those figures part ways.

If you are a seller facing a buyer's low appraisal, the same logic runs in reverse. Sometimes meeting partway keeps a good, already-committed buyer versus restarting weeks of days on market with no guarantee the next appraisal lands higher. We help you see the whole board before you decide.
highlight: Before you panic over a low appraisal, read your own contract first. The contingencies you kept or waived decide almost everything about your next move. Then negotiate with comparable sales, not feelings.
Daniel Cope, Real Estate Broker, Your Realty Link
faqs: Does a low appraisal mean I am overpaying?

Not necessarily. An appraisal is one licensed opinion based on recent comparable sales, and in a fast market those comps can lag real value. It is a data point to weigh, not proof the home is not worth it to you.
Can I just get a second appraisal?

Usually the lender controls the appraisal, so you cannot shop around for a higher number on the same loan. You can request a reconsideration of value with better comps, and in some cases switching lenders means a new appraisal, but confirm the specifics with your loan officer.
Who pays for the appraisal?
The buyer typically pays for the appraisal as part of the loan process, and that cost generally is not refundable even if the value comes in low. Ask your lender for the exact amount up front.

seo_title: Home Inspection Red Flags Indianapolis | Your Realty Link
meta_desc: Know the home inspection red flags that matter most for Indianapolis buyers, from foundations to radon, plus how to negotiate repairs after the report.
h1: Home Inspection Red Flags Every Indy Buyer Should Know
hero_sub: From century-old bungalows to brand-new builds, Central Indiana homes hide different problems. Learn which inspection findings are routine and which deserve a hard second look.
schema_headline: Home Inspection Red Flags in Indianapolis
schema_desc: A Central Indiana buyer's guide to the home inspection red flags that matter most and how to negotiate repairs.
intro: Picture yourself in the driveway of a 1920s bungalow in Irvington, keys almost in hand, when the inspector waves you toward the basement. This is the moment a purchase gets real. A home inspection is your one scheduled chance to look past fresh paint and staging and understand what you are actually buying. In Central Indiana, where the housing stock ranges from century-old near-north-side homes to brand-new builds in Hancock County, knowing which findings are routine and which are true red flags can save you thousands of dollars and a lot of heartache. Here is how to read your inspection like a pro.
sections: what-inspection-covers
What a Home Inspection Actually Covers

A general home inspection is a top-to-bottom visual review of the home's major systems and structure — roof, foundation, framing, electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling, insulation, drainage, and the visible condition of walls, floors, windows, and doors. The inspector is not tearing open walls; they report on what can be seen and safely accessed.

You will receive a written report, usually with photos, sorting findings by urgency. Most reports run long and list dozens of items. That length is normal and does not mean the home is a lemon — even a solid house generates a long list because a good inspector documents everything, right down to a loose railing or a worn washer.

Plan to attend if you can, at least for the final walkthrough. Standing in the crawl space with the inspector teaches you more than any PDF ever will. Bring your questions and ask them to point out what is urgent, what is routine, and what they would keep an eye on.
red-flags
Red Flags That Matter Most in Indy-Area Homes
Every home has quirks, but a handful of issues carry outsized weight in Central Indiana because of our soil, our weather, and our older neighborhoods. These are the findings worth slowing down for.

• Foundation and settling: Indiana's clay-heavy soils expand and contract with moisture. Horizontal cracks, bowing basement walls, or doors that will not close can signal movement worth a structural engineer's opinion.
  • Roof age and condition: Ask how many years of life are left. A roof near the end of its span is a major near-term expense.
  • Aging furnace and HVAC: Our real winters and humid summers work these systems hard. An older furnace or air conditioner may run today but sit close to replacement.
  • Water in basements and crawl spaces: Standing water, chalky efflorescence, a musty smell, or a failed sump pump all point to drainage problems that invite mold and rot.
  • Older wiring: In historic pockets like Irvington and the near-north side, you may find knob-and-tube or ungrounded wiring, or an overloaded panel that needs updating for safety and insurance.
  • Sewer line issues: Older clay laterals and mature tree roots are a classic Indy combination. A separate sewer scope can reveal cracks or blockages before they become a costly dig.

Not every one of these kills a deal. But each deserves a closer look, often from a specialist, before you decide how to move forward. A scary line item on paper often turns into a manageable number once a pro takes a real look.
normal-vs-problem
Normal Wear Versus a Real Problem

The art of reading an inspection is separating cosmetic, routine wear from structural or safety concerns. A dripping faucet, worn caulk, a few cracked driveway sections, or a handful of dead outlets are maintenance items — annoying, inexpensive, and expected in a lived-in home. A cracked heat exchanger, active water intrusion, or a foundation that is moving is a completely different category.

Compare the inspection against the seller's disclosure, the form where Indiana sellers report known defects. If the inspector finds an issue the seller marked as no problem, that is worth a direct conversation. It may be an honest oversight, or it may change how you approach the negotiation.

When in doubt, get a specialist quote. A roofer, HVAC technician, structural engineer, or plumber can turn a vague, alarming note into a firm dollar figure, which is exactly what you need to negotiate with confidence rather than fear.
radon
Do Not Skip the Radon Test

Radon is an invisible, odorless radioactive gas that seeps up from soil and rock, and it is the one hazard many Indiana buyers overlook. Much of Indiana falls within the EPA's highest-risk radon zone, which makes testing a genuinely smart move here regardless of the neighborhood or the home's age.

A radon test is inexpensive relative to the peace of mind it buys, and it is usually ordered alongside the general inspection. If levels come back elevated, the fix is typically a mitigation system that vents the gas safely away from the home — a solvable and often negotiable problem. Confirm current guidance and action levels with the Indiana State Department of Health or a certified radon professional rather than relying on rules of thumb.
Do not assume a newer home is automatically safe. Radon depends on the ground beneath the house, not the year it was built. Test regardless, and you will know rather than guess.
negotiating-repairs
Negotiating Repairs After the Inspection

In most Central Indiana purchase agreements, your power to act on the inspection comes from the inspection contingency. This clause gives you a defined window to review the report and respond — by requesting repairs, asking for a credit, renegotiating the price, or walking away if the two sides cannot agree.

Smart negotiating means picking your battles. Bundling every minor item tends to frustrate sellers and dilute your real ask. Focusing on health, safety, and big-ticket structural or mechanical findings lands far better. Your options generally include:

• Seller makes the repairs: Completed with agreed contractors before closing.
  • Seller credit: A closing-cost credit so you control the repair after you own the home.
  • Price reduction: A lower price that reflects the work needed.
  • Walk away: Exercising the contingency to cancel and protect your earnest money if the issues are simply too big.
should-you-waive
Should You Ever Waive an Inspection?

In competitive stretches, some buyers waive the inspection to make an offer stand out. Be careful. Waiving it means giving up your best window to discover expensive problems before you are legally committed. For most buyers, and especially first-timers, that risk is not worth it.

An as-is sale is a related but different situation. As-is means the seller will not make repairs, but in most cases you can still inspect for your own information and still keep the right to walk away based on what you find. Read your contract carefully, because the exact wording matters.

If you feel pressure to waive, talk to your agent about alternatives such as a shorter inspection window, an information-only inspection, or a cap on the repairs you will request. There is usually a middle path that keeps your offer strong without leaving you blind. If you are early in the process, our first-time home buyer guide for Indianapolis shows how inspections fit the bigger timeline, and because major findings can echo into the lender's valuation, it is worth understanding what hurts a home appraisal in Indiana too.
highlight: Read every inspection report by category, not by length. A two-page list of maintenance items is usually a healthy home, while one line about a moving foundation is the sentence that deserves your full attention.
Daniel Cope, Real Estate Broker, Your Realty Link
faqs: How long does a home inspection take in Indianapolis?
Most general inspections run a few hours depending on the size and age of the home. Plan to join for at least the final walkthrough so the inspector can show you the findings in person.
Is a home inspection required to buy a home in Indiana?
No, it is not legally required, and a cash buyer can waive it. But it is strongly recommended, because it is your main chance to find costly problems before you are committed.
Should I get a separate radon and sewer test?
Often yes. A general inspection does not always include radon testing or a sewer scope, and both catch expensive Indiana-specific problems. Ask your inspector which add-ons they offer.

seo_title: Pre-Approval vs Pre-Qualification | Your Realty Link
meta_desc: Pre-approval versus pre-qualification confuses many Indianapolis buyers. Learn the real difference, why it wins offers, and how to get pre-approved fast.
hero_sub: In a fast Central Indiana market, a verified pre-approval can decide whether your offer even gets read. Here is how it differs from a quick pre-qualification.
schema_desc: A clear explanation of pre-approval versus pre-qualification and why it matters for Indianapolis home buyers.
intro: You have been scrolling homes online for weeks, and a listing in Greenwood finally checks every box. You call to see it, and the first thing the agent asks is, are you pre-approved? If you are not sure whether the number your lender's app gave you counts, you are not alone. The difference between pre-approval and pre-qualification confuses a lot of Central Indiana buyers, and in a market where good homes move fast, it is a distinction that can decide whether your offer even gets read. Here is what separates the two and why it matters.
sections: two-terms
Pre-Qualification and Pre-Approval Are Not the Same

Pre-qualification is the quick, informal first step. You tell a lender your income, debts, and assets, they run a rough estimate, and you get a ballpark of what you might afford. It is fast, often done online in minutes, and it usually does not involve verifying anything you said. It is useful for orientation, not for making a serious offer.

Pre-approval is the real deal. The lender collects and verifies your documents, checks your credit, and issues a written commitment to lend up to a specific amount, subject to the property and final underwriting. It carries genuine weight because a professional has actually vetted your finances rather than taking your word for it.
Think of pre-qualification as a rough sketch and pre-approval as a signed blueprint. Both have a place early on, but only one tells a seller you are truly ready to close.
why-it-matters
Why Pre-Approval Wins in a Competitive Market

In desirable Central Indiana pockets — parts of Hamilton County, established Marion County neighborhoods, and the growing suburbs of Hendricks and Johnson counties — well-priced homes can attract multiple offers quickly. Listing agents and sellers screen offers partly by how likely they are to actually close, and a verified pre-approval signals a low-risk buyer.

An offer with no pre-approval letter, or with only a flimsy pre-qualification, can get set aside in favor of a buyer who has done the work. In a tight situation, that is often the difference between touring your dream home and hearing it went to someone else.

Pre-approval protects you, too. Knowing your true, verified budget keeps you from falling for a home you cannot finance, and it clears the path to closing once you are under contract. You shop with confidence instead of hoping the numbers work out later.
documents
What Documents You Will Need
Getting pre-approved means giving your lender a real look at your finances. Exact requirements vary by lender and loan program, but be ready to provide most of the following.

• Proof of income: Recent pay stubs, and often W-2s or tax returns, especially if you are self-employed.
  • Bank and asset statements: To document your down payment and cash reserves.
  • Identification: A government-issued ID and typically your Social Security number for a credit check.
  • Employment verification: Your lender may contact your employer directly to confirm your job.
  • Debt details: Information on car loans, student loans, and credit cards so the lender can calculate your ratios.

Gathering these early is one of the smartest things a buyer can do. The faster your lender has clean, complete documents, the stronger and quicker your pre-approval — and the more confidently you can act the moment the right listing appears.
stronger-offer
How Pre-Approval Strengthens Your Offer

When you make an offer, your pre-approval letter travels with it and tells the seller a lender already stands behind you. Paired with a reasonable earnest money deposit — the good-faith funds you put down to show you are serious — it forms the backbone of a credible offer.

A verified pre-approval also lets you build a cleaner contingency structure. Because your financing is largely vetted, you and your agent can set realistic timelines and, where it makes sense, present terms that reassure the seller without exposing you to undue risk. That combination often beats a slightly higher offer from a shakier buyer.

The reverse is true as well. If your financing later falls apart because your pre-approval was thin, you can jeopardize your earnest money and the entire deal. Doing the pre-approval right up front protects the money you put on the line and the home you want to keep.
loan-types
Loan Types and What Pre-Approval Tells You

During pre-approval, your lender helps match you to a loan program that fits your finances and goals. Options in Indiana commonly include conventional, FHA, VA, and USDA loans, each with its own guidelines. A conventional loan is a common starting point for buyers with solid credit and a down payment, though it is far from the only path.

Your down payment size shapes more than the loan amount. With many programs, putting down less than a lender's threshold means paying private mortgage insurance, an added monthly cost that protects the lender rather than you. Pre-approval is when you learn whether that applies to your situation and how it affects your monthly payment, so there are no surprises later.

We keep loan-type talk general on purpose, because the right fit depends on your credit, savings, and plans — details a licensed lender should confirm. If a smaller down payment is your reality, our guide to down payment assistance programs in Indiana is a smart next read.
next-steps
Getting Pre-Approved With Your Realty Link

A strong pre-approval is a team effort between you, a trustworthy local lender, and an agent who knows how to translate it into a winning offer. Janet Giles-Schultz, Principal Broker, and the Your Realty Link team work with buyers across the MIBOR MLS and can connect you with reputable Central Indiana lenders who close on time.

Once you are pre-approved, you can search with real focus. When you are ready to browse active listings, use the Your Realty Link property search at yourrealtylink.com/property-search, and we will help you write an offer that stands up in a competitive market.
New to all of this? Our first-time home buyer guide for Indianapolis lays out every step from pre-approval to keys in hand, so you always know what comes next.
highlight: Get fully pre-approved before you fall in love with a house, not after. It sets your real budget, sharpens your search, and makes your offer one a seller can actually trust.
Daniel Cope, Real Estate Broker, Your Realty Link
faqs: How long does a mortgage pre-approval last?
Pre-approvals are typically valid for a limited number of months before the lender needs updated documents. Ask your lender for their exact window and what it takes to renew it.
Does getting pre-approved hurt my credit?

A pre-approval usually involves a hard credit inquiry, which can have a small, temporary effect. Shopping several lenders in a short window is generally treated as one inquiry, so confirm the timing with your loan officer.
Can I make an offer without pre-approval?
In most competitive Central Indiana situations, sellers expect a pre-approval letter with the offer. Going without one puts you at a real disadvantage against buyers who have done the work.

seo_title: Earnest Money in Indiana Explained | Your Realty Link
meta_desc: Earnest money in Indiana explained for buyers: how much is typical, who holds your deposit, when you get it back, and when you could forfeit it in a home sale.
h1: Earnest Money in Indiana: What Every Buyer Should Know
hero_sub: The good-faith deposit every Indiana buyer makes, demystified. Here is how much is typical, who holds it, and exactly when you get it back.
schema_headline: Earnest Money in Indiana: What Every Buyer Should Know
schema_desc: A plain-English guide to earnest money for Indiana home buyers, covering how much is typical, who holds it, and when you get it back or lose it.
intro: If you are buying a home in Central Indiana, one of the first checks you will write is your earnest money deposit. For a lot of first-time buyers, that moment feels a little nerve-wracking, because you are handing over real money before you own anything. The good news is that earnest money is one of the most misunderstood, and most recoverable, parts of an Indiana purchase agreement. In this guide I will walk you through what earnest money is, how much is typical around Indianapolis, who actually holds it, when you get it back, and the few situations where you could lose it.
sections: what-is-earnest-money
What Earnest Money Actually Is

Earnest money is a good-faith deposit you make when you sign a purchase agreement on a home. Think of it as a way of telling the seller, in a language they trust, that you are serious about following through. When a seller accepts your offer, they take their home off the market and stop entertaining other buyers, sometimes for weeks. Your earnest money is the assurance that you are not going to walk away casually while they turn everyone else down. In Central Indiana's active market, that signal carries real weight with sellers.

It is important to understand that earnest money is not a fee, and it is not extra money you simply lose. In almost every normal transaction it becomes part of what you were already going to pay. It just gets deposited early and held by a neutral party until closing. If you are new to all of this, our first-time home buyer guide for Indianapolis walks through the full process. The short version is reassuring: in the vast majority of Indiana deals, your earnest money does not disappear.
how-much
How Much Earnest Money Is Typical Around Indianapolis

There is no fixed earnest money amount required by Indiana law, and the number you offer can be a small strategy conversation of its own. As a general rule, earnest money is usually a modest percentage of the purchase price, though it truly varies from deal to deal. In a calm situation with little competition, a smaller deposit is often perfectly acceptable. In a competitive multiple-offer situation, which happens often in sought-after Hamilton County suburbs, buyers sometimes offer more to signal strength and stand out.
A few things influence what makes sense for your particular offer:

• Local competition: In hot Hamilton and Boone County submarkets, a stronger deposit can help your offer get noticed.
  • Price point: A percentage of a higher-priced home is naturally a larger dollar figure.
  • Seller expectations: Some sellers, especially on new construction, ask for a specific deposit up front.
  • Your comfort level: It should be enough to be credible, but never more than you can responsibly put up.

Whatever figure you land on, remember that earnest money is refundable in the normal course of a well-written deal. You are not gambling it away by offering a bit more to win a home you love; you are simply front-loading part of your down payment. A good agent will help you calibrate the amount so your offer is competitive without overextending you.
who-holds-it
Who Actually Holds Your Earnest Money

Here is the part that reassures most buyers: your earnest money does not go into the seller's pocket. It is held by a neutral third party in escrow, typically an escrow or title company, or sometimes a real estate broker's trust account. That neutral party cannot simply hand the money to either side on a whim. It is released only according to the terms spelled out in your purchase agreement, which keeps everyone honest.

This neutral-holder setup is exactly why earnest money works as a good-faith tool without putting you at unfair risk. The title company in your transaction keeps a clean record of the deposit and applies it at the closing table. If you are working with a MIBOR member agent, they will make sure the deposit is delivered to the right place on time and documented properly. Part of that same representation is understanding how the buyer compensation agreement works in Indiana, so you know who is being paid and how.

One practical tip: always follow the delivery instructions in your contract exactly, and keep your receipt or wire confirmation. Earnest money disputes are rare in Indiana, but when questions do come up, a clear paper trail showing where the money went and when settles them fast.
get-it-back
When You Get Your Earnest Money Back

In an Indiana purchase agreement, your ability to get your earnest money back usually comes down to your contingencies. A contingency is a condition that has to be met for the sale to move forward, and if it is not met, it generally gives you a defined way to cancel and recover your deposit. These are your safety valves, and they are one of the biggest reasons to have solid representation on your side of the table.
The most common contingencies that can protect your deposit include:

• Inspection: If the home inspection turns up problems you and the seller cannot resolve, you can typically walk away within the agreed window.
  • Financing: If your loan falls through despite a genuine good-faith effort, a financing contingency generally lets you cancel.
  • Appraisal: If the home appraises below the agreed price and the gap cannot be worked out, this contingency can protect you.
forfeit
When You Could Lose Your Earnest Money

The flip side is real: earnest money can be forfeited. The most common way buyers lose their deposit is by walking away from a deal for a reason that is not covered by a contingency, simply changing their mind after all the protective windows have closed. At that point, the seller has held the home off the market in reliance on your commitment, and the deposit is what compensates them for that lost time and opportunity.

Missing deadlines is the other big risk. Contingency windows have firm dates, and if you let an inspection or financing deadline pass without acting, you can quietly lose the protection that would have let you cancel. This is also why the final walk-through and every earlier deadline matter so much, and why you want an agent actively tracking those dates for you. Stay inside your contingencies and hit your deadlines, and forfeiting your earnest money becomes very unlikely.
at-closing
How Earnest Money Gets Credited at Closing

Assuming everything goes the way it should, your earnest money is not lost at all. At closing, it is credited toward what you owe, usually applied to your down payment or your closing costs. In other words, that early check simply becomes part of the money you were always going to bring to the table, and your final cash-to-close figure is reduced by the amount you already put down. It is one of the nicer surprises at the closing table for first-time buyers.

The closing statement will show the deposit as a credit on your side of the ledger, and the title company reconciles it against the total. If for some reason the deal is properly canceled under a contingency, the same paperwork trail is what gets your money returned cleanly and promptly. Either way, keeping good records and working with a broker who understands the process end to end is how you make sure that deposit does exactly what it is supposed to do.

If you take one thing from this guide, let it be this: earnest money is a promise you can keep and get back. Understand your contingencies, respect your deadlines, and lean on your agent, and that deposit becomes a smooth, ordinary part of buying your home rather than something to lose sleep over.
highlight: Your earnest money is a promise, not a fee. Keep your contingencies in place and hit every deadline, and in almost every Indiana deal that deposit simply becomes part of your down payment.
Daniel Cope, Real Estate Broker, Your Realty Link
faqs: Is earnest money required to buy a home in Indiana?
It is not required by law, but sellers almost always expect a deposit as a sign of good faith. Skipping it can make your offer look weak, especially in a competitive market.
Where does my earnest money go after I write the check?
It is held by a neutral party such as an escrow or title company, or a broker's trust account, not by the seller. It stays there until closing or until the deal is properly canceled.
Will I lose my earnest money if my loan is denied?
Usually not, as long as you have a financing contingency and you made a genuine good-faith effort to get approved. Talk with your lender and agent early so you protect that contingency.

meta_desc: Indiana property tax caps explained: the 1, 2, and 3 percent circuit breaker limits, how the homestead cap works, and what investors and buyers should know.
hero_sub: Indiana's constitutional circuit breaker puts a hard ceiling on your property tax bill. Here is how the 1, 2, and 3 percent caps really work.
schema_desc: How Indiana's constitutional 1, 2, and 3 percent property tax caps work, who qualifies for the homestead cap, and what investors should know.
intro: One of the quiet advantages of owning a home in Indiana is something written right into the state constitution: property tax caps. Often called the circuit breaker, these caps put a hard ceiling on your property tax bill based on the value of your property. For buyers moving to the Indianapolis area from other states, this is genuinely good news, because it makes your future tax bill more predictable. In this guide I will explain how the 1 percent, 2 percent, and 3 percent caps work, who qualifies for the lowest cap, what investors should know, and where to confirm the details that change.
sections: what-are-caps
What Indiana's Property Tax Caps Are

Indiana's property tax caps are a constitutional limit on how much you can be charged in property tax relative to your property's gross assessed value. The system is nicknamed the circuit breaker because, like the breaker in your electrical panel, it stops the bill from climbing past a set point. These are not a temporary program or a local ordinance that can vanish next year. They were added to the Indiana Constitution by voter referendum, which is a big reason they are so stable and dependable.

There are three cap levels, and the one that applies to you depends on how the property is classified. The three tiers are 1 percent for an owner-occupied homestead, 2 percent for other residential property and farmland, and 3 percent for commercial and business property. Understanding which bucket your property falls into is the key to knowing your ceiling, so let's walk through each one.

Because the caps are constitutional, they give Hoosier homeowners a rare kind of certainty. Local rates and assessments can move, but the ceiling relative to your assessed value stays put. That is the mental model to carry with you: the caps set the maximum, and the deductions and credits determine how far below that maximum your actual bill lands.
one-percent
The 1 Percent Cap for Your Homestead

If you own and live in your home as your primary residence, you fall under the 1 percent cap. This means your property tax bill is limited to 1 percent of the gross assessed value of your homestead. On a home assessed at a given value, that ceiling is straightforward to estimate, and it is the lowest of the three caps, which rewards owner-occupants who put down roots.

The catch is that you have to claim it. The 1 percent cap is tied to filing for your homestead exemption with your county. If you buy a home and never file the homestead paperwork, you can miss out on the lowest cap and the deductions that go with it. We walk buyers and sellers through this constantly, and it is the subject of our deeper guide on the Indiana homestead exemption and how it lowers property taxes. If you just bought, confirm your filing with the county auditor.

The homestead filing is not something to put off. In many Indiana counties you file once and it carries forward, but you have to get it on record first. If you bought recently and are not certain it was handled, a quick call to your county auditor is well worth your time. Getting the 1 percent cap in place protects your budget from day one of ownership.
two-three
The 2 Percent and 3 Percent Caps

The 2 percent cap covers other residential property and agricultural land. This is where a rental house, a second home, or a home that is not your primary residence generally lands. The ceiling is 2 percent of gross assessed value rather than 1 percent, so the same assessed value can carry a higher tax ceiling when the property is not your homestead.
The 3 percent cap applies to commercial and business property, including most nonresidential real estate. Here is a simple way to remember the whole system:

• 1 percent: Owner-occupied homestead, your primary residence.
  • 2 percent: Other residential and farmland, including rentals and second homes.
  • 3 percent: Commercial and business property.

Notice that the jump from your homestead to a rental is not small in percentage terms, even though it sounds like just one point. For a property of the same assessed value, the 2 percent ceiling is double the 1 percent ceiling, which is why classification matters so much to your bottom line.
investors
What the Caps Mean for Investors and Second Homes

For real estate investors, the difference between the 1 percent and 2 percent caps matters a lot to your numbers. A rental property in Marion or Hancock County falls under the 2 percent cap because it is not owner-occupied, so your carrying costs are calculated against that higher ceiling. It is not a penalty so much as a classification, but you should build it into your projections from day one.

This also affects how you think about a property you might convert. If you turn a former primary residence into a rental, its cap classification can change, which affects both cash flow and the home equity math over time. If you are weighing owning versus renting for yourself, our comparison of renting versus buying in Indianapolis lays out how predictable ownership costs, including capped taxes, factor into the decision.

If you are running the numbers on a rental in Marion, Hancock, or Johnson County, build the 2 percent ceiling into your model before you make an offer, not after. It is a small step that keeps your projected cash flow honest and your expectations grounded.
deductions-credits
Deductions and Credits Change, So Confirm the Details

Here is the part where I have to be careful and honest with you. While the 1, 2, and 3 percent caps themselves are constitutional and stable, the deductions and credits that reduce your assessed value and your bill are set by the legislature, and those get adjusted. Indiana lawmakers made changes affecting property tax relief in 2025, and the specific deduction amounts and any credits can shift from year to year.
Because of that, I am not going to quote you a specific deduction dollar figure, since it could be out of date by the time you read this. Instead, do this:

• Confirm current deductions: Check the latest homestead and supplemental deduction amounts with your county auditor.
  • Check for credits: Ask about any current property tax credits you may qualify for.
  • Use official sources: The Indiana Department of Local Government Finance, the DLGF, publishes current guidance.
why-matters
Why the Caps Matter When You Buy

When you are shopping for a home, the tax cap gives you a dependable way to sanity-check your monthly budget. Because the ceiling is tied to assessed value and your homestead status, you can estimate a realistic upper bound on the tax portion of your payment before you ever make an offer. That predictability is one of the reasons Central Indiana remains attractive to buyers coming from higher-tax states.

It also underscores why working with a knowledgeable local agent pays off. A MIBOR member agent with Your Realty Link can help you understand how a specific property is classified, remind you to file your homestead, and point you to the county resources that keep your numbers current. Janet Giles-Schultz, our Principal Broker, has guided countless Indianapolis-area families through exactly these details, and getting them right early can save real money over the life of your ownership.

None of this replaces personalized tax advice, and I am not offering that here. What the caps give you is a dependable framework, a known ceiling you can build a budget around, which is more than buyers get in a lot of other states. Pair that framework with current numbers from the county, and you can shop with real confidence.
highlight: The 1 percent cap is one of the best deals in Indiana homeownership, but only if you file your homestead. Do that paperwork the moment you close, then confirm your current deductions with the county.
Daniel Cope, Real Estate Broker, Your Realty Link
faqs: Are Indiana's property tax caps permanent?

The 1, 2, and 3 percent caps are written into the Indiana Constitution, which makes them very stable. The deductions and credits that reduce your bill are set by the legislature and can change, so confirm those each year.
Do I automatically get the 1 percent cap when I buy a home?
Not automatically. You need to file for the homestead on your primary residence with your county. If you skip it, you can end up taxed at a higher effective rate.
Why is my rental property taxed at a higher cap?
Rentals and second homes are not owner-occupied, so they fall under the 2 percent cap instead of the 1 percent homestead cap. Factor that into your investment numbers.
cta_h3: Know your numbers before you buy or sell.
cta_p: Understanding your tax ceiling is just one piece of the picture. Start with a clear, current sense of what your home is worth, and let Your Realty Link help you plan your next move with confidence.

seo_title: Using Home Equity to Buy Your Next Home | Your Realty Link
meta_desc: Learn how Central Indiana homeowners use home equity to buy their next home: sale proceeds, sell first vs buy first, and how to start by knowing your number.
h1: Using Home Equity to Buy Your Next Home
hero_sub: Years in your home may have built more buying power than you think. Here is how to turn Central Indiana equity into your next move.
schema_headline: Using Home Equity to Buy Your Next Home in Indianapolis
schema_desc: How Central Indiana homeowners can use built-up equity to fund the down payment on their next home and decide whether to sell first or buy first.
intro: If you have owned a home in the Indianapolis area for a while, you may be sitting on more buying power than you realize. That buying power is your home equity, and for a lot of Central Indiana homeowners it has quietly become the key that unlocks the next move, whether that is a bigger house in Fishers, a ranch closer to the grandkids, or a lake place near Geist. In this guide I will explain what equity is, how homeowners here have built it, and the practical ways you can put it to work on your next home.
sections: what-is-equity
What Home Equity Really Is

Home equity is simply the difference between what your home is worth today and what you still owe on your mortgage. If your home would sell for a certain amount and your loan balance is lower than that, the gap is your equity. It is real wealth, and it is yours, even though it is tied up in the house until you either sell or borrow against it.

Two forces grow your equity over time. The first is paying down your loan balance, month after month, which slowly shifts more of the home into the owned column. The second is appreciation, meaning the home's value rising over the years. For many Indianapolis-area owners, both have been working in their favor at the same time, which is why so many people are surprised, in a good way, when they find out where they stand.

Because equity is tied to your home's current value, it is not a fixed number you set once. It moves as the market moves and as you pay down your loan. That is why any serious conversation about using equity has to start with a fresh, realistic valuation rather than a figure you remember from your last refinance.
how-built
How Indy-Area Homeowners Build Equity

Central Indiana has been a steady, sensible housing market for a long time, and that steadiness is exactly what builds equity. I am not going to throw specific appreciation percentages at you, because those change and get stale fast. What I can tell you is that homeowners across Marion, Hamilton, Johnson, and Hendricks counties who bought and simply stayed put have generally watched their ownership stake grow year over year.
A few ordinary things quietly build equity for Indy-area owners:

• Regular payments: Each mortgage payment chips away at your principal balance.
  • Time in the home: The longer you own, the more principal you pay and the more appreciation can add up.
  • Smart improvements: Sensible updates can support your home's value at resale.
  • A stable local market: Central Indiana's steady demand has supported values over time.

The encouraging reality for longtime owners is that you may have far more equity than your monthly statement suggests, because that statement shows your loan balance but not your home's current market value. The only way to see the full picture is to look at both sides at once.
sale-proceeds
Turning Sale Proceeds Into Your Next Down Payment

The most common way homeowners use equity is the most straightforward: you sell your current home, pay off the remaining mortgage, and the proceeds left over become the down payment on your next one. For move-up buyers, this is powerful, because years of built-up equity can translate into a substantial down payment on the next house.

A bigger down payment does more than lower your loan amount. Putting down a healthy chunk can help you avoid private mortgage insurance, which reduces your monthly payment, and it can make your offer more competitive to a seller. In a market where sellers weigh how solid each offer is, walking in with strong equity behind you is a real advantage that a good agent will help you present well.

For sellers stepping up to a larger home, this is often the cleanest path. You are not borrowing against the old house or juggling extra products; you are simply moving your accumulated equity from one property to the next in a single, well-timed transaction.
sell-first-buy-first
Sell First or Buy First? The Central Indiana Trade-Off

Here is the question almost every equity-rich homeowner wrestles with: do I sell first or buy first? Both paths are common in Central Indiana, and both have real trade-offs. Selling first means you know exactly how much equity you have to work with and you are not carrying two mortgages, but it can leave you needing a temporary place to live if you cannot line up the timing.

Buying first means you can move once, on your schedule, without a gap, but it can stretch you financially in the window before your current home sells, and it may lean on tools like a bridge loan. There is no universally right answer. The best choice depends on your finances, your timeline, and how the local market is behaving when you make your move. This is exactly the kind of decision where sitting down with an experienced broker pays off, because we can map the timing to your specific situation.
tap-equity
Other Ways to Tap Your Equity

Selling is not the only way to access equity. Some homeowners want to keep their current home, or pull cash for a down payment before they sell, and there are lending tools designed for that. I am going to keep this general and stay away from quoting rates or specific terms, because those move constantly and depend on your lender and your profile. At a high level, homeowners commonly consider two routes:

• A home equity line of credit: A revolving line secured by your home that you can draw against as needed.
  • A cash-out refinance: Replacing your existing mortgage with a larger one and taking the difference in cash.

Each of these has costs, risks, and qualification requirements, and the right fit depends entirely on your numbers. Talk with a trusted lender about current options, and loop in your agent so the strategy lines up with your actual buying and selling plan.
know-your-number
Start by Knowing Your Number

Every one of these strategies starts with the same first step: knowing your number. You cannot plan a move, size a down payment, or decide between selling first and buying first until you have a realistic, current picture of what your home is worth. Guessing high leads to disappointment, and guessing low can cost you thousands in buying power you did not know you had.

The best way to get that number is a comparative market analysis from a local agent who actually knows your neighborhood, not an automated estimate that has never set foot in your home. If you want to understand the difference, our post on CMA versus Zestimate in Indianapolis breaks it down, and our guide on what your home is worth in Indianapolis goes deeper. Keep in mind that a lender's home appraisal later in the process is a separate, formal valuation.

When you are ready, Janet Giles-Schultz and the MIBOR member team at Your Realty Link will give you a straight, well-supported estimate of your equity and help you build a plan around it. Knowing your number is free, it is low-pressure, and it turns a vague sense of maybe we could move into a concrete, confident next step.
highlight: Before you fall in love with your next house, get a real, local read on your current one. Your equity is the foundation of the whole move, and knowing it turns wishful thinking into a workable plan.
Daniel Cope, Real Estate Broker, Your Realty Link
faqs: How do I know how much equity I have in my Indianapolis home?
Start with a comparative market analysis from a local agent to estimate your home's current value, then subtract your remaining mortgage balance. That gap is your approximate equity.
Should I sell my current home before buying the next one?

It depends on your finances and timing. Selling first gives you certainty about your equity and avoids two mortgages, while buying first lets you move once. A local broker can help you weigh the trade-offs.
Can I use my equity without selling my home?
Yes, tools like a home equity line of credit or a cash-out refinance let you tap equity while keeping the home. Terms vary, so talk with a trusted lender about current options.
cta_h3: Ready to put your equity to work?
cta_p: It starts with knowing your number. Get a free, no-pressure home valuation from Your Realty Link, and let's map out how your equity can fund your next move in Central Indiana.

seo_title: Buying a Home With an HOA in Indiana | Your Realty Link
meta_desc: Buying an HOA home in the Indianapolis suburbs? Learn what dues cover, which rules to expect, and the documents to review before you close on a house.
h1: Buying a Home With an HOA in Central Indiana
hero_sub: Homeowners associations are everywhere in the Indianapolis suburbs. Here is what to understand about dues, rules, and documents before you buy.
schema_headline: Buying a Home With an HOA in Central Indiana
schema_desc: A Central Indiana buyer's guide to homeowners associations, including dues, covenants, and the HOA documents to review before closing.
intro: If you are house hunting in the Central Indiana suburbs, there is a very good chance the home you fall in love with belongs to a homeowners association. From the newer neighborhoods in Fishers and Westfield to the growing communities in Brownsburg, Whitestown, and McCordsville, HOAs are simply part of suburban life here. They are not something to fear, but they are something to understand before you sign. This guide walks through what an HOA is, what your dues pay for, the rules that come with the territory, and the documents you should read closely before you commit.
sections: what-is-hoa
What an HOA Actually Is

A homeowners association, or HOA, is a private organization that manages and governs a residential community. When you buy in an HOA neighborhood, you automatically become a member, and membership is not optional. The association is typically run by a volunteer board of homeowners, often with help from a professional management company, and it is funded by the dues that every owner pays. Its job is to maintain shared spaces, enforce community standards, and protect property values across the neighborhood.

Here in Central Indiana, HOAs show up most often in newer subdivisions, planned communities, condos, and townhome developments. If you are drawn to the amenity-rich neighborhoods going up around Westfield, Noblesville, and Whitestown, an HOA is almost a given. Buyers exploring the many new construction communities in the Indianapolis suburbs should expect one, since builders establish the association as part of developing the neighborhood. Older, established Indianapolis neighborhoods are less likely to have a mandatory HOA, though some have voluntary neighborhood groups you can choose to join.
dues-cover
What Your HOA Dues Typically Cover

HOA dues vary widely from one community to the next, and they can be billed monthly, quarterly, or annually. A single-family neighborhood with a shared entrance and a couple of common areas will sit at the lower end. A community with a pool, clubhouse, fitness center, and miles of walking trails will cost more, because those amenities take real money to maintain. Condo and townhome associations tend to charge the most, because their dues often cover exterior building maintenance that a single-family owner would handle on their own.

• Common area upkeep: mowing, mulching, and maintaining the shared green spaces, islands, and entrances.
  • Amenities: the pool, clubhouse, playground, trails, and fitness areas many Hamilton County communities are known for.
  • Stormwater and retention ponds: the drainage infrastructure that keeps a neighborhood functioning is often an HOA responsibility.
  • Neighborhood entrance and signage: lighting, landscaping, and seasonal decor at the community entrance.
  • Exterior maintenance and trash: in many condo and townhome associations, roofs, siding, and trash service are bundled in.

It is worth asking exactly what your dues include, because the answer shapes your true monthly cost of ownership. Two homes with the same price can carry very different HOA obligations, and that difference belongs in your budget from day one rather than as a surprise after you move in.
rules-covenants
The Rules and Covenants You Are Agreeing To

Every HOA operates under a set of governing documents, and the most important of these are the Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions, usually shortened to CC and Rs. These are recorded rules that run with the land, which means they apply to you the moment you take ownership. They exist to keep the neighborhood consistent and protect resale value, but they can also limit things you might assume are entirely your call.

• Exterior appearance: paint colors, roofing materials, and landscaping choices often require approval.
  • Fences and structures: fence height and style, sheds, and additions frequently need board sign-off.
  • Parking: rules on street parking, boats, RVs, and commercial vehicles are common.
  • Leasing and rentals: some associations cap how many homes can be rented, which matters if you ever want to lease yours.
  • Everyday details: basketball hoops, satellite dishes, flags, and even holiday decorations can be regulated.

None of this is necessarily bad. The same rules that stop your neighbor from parking a boat on the lawn also protect your view and your value. The point is simply to read the CC and Rs before closing so nothing surprises you. If a particular restriction would be a dealbreaker for how you plan to live, it is far better to learn that now. The seller disclosure may hint at association obligations, but the governing documents are where the real detail lives.
review-documents
Read the HOA Documents During Your Contingency Window

This is the single most important step, and it is the one buyers most often rush. When you are under contract, you have a window to investigate the home before your commitment becomes final. That same window is your chance to review the HOA's documents. Use your contingency period to request and actually read the association's financials, not just the rulebook.

Pay attention to the budget and, especially, the reserve fund. Reserves are the savings an association sets aside for big-ticket repairs like repaving roads or replacing a pool. An underfunded reserve is a warning sign, because it often means a special assessment is coming, and that is a bill every owner has to pay. Read the recent meeting minutes for talk of lawsuits, major projects, or dues increases, and ask directly whether any special assessments are planned.

Line this review up alongside your home inspection. While your inspector evaluates the physical condition of the house, you evaluate the financial and legal health of the association. Both protect you, and both belong inside your investigation window. If the documents are hard to get or the numbers look thin, that itself tells you something important before you are locked in.
pros-cons
The Pros and Cons of HOA Living

HOA living is a genuine trade-off, and reasonable buyers land on both sides of it. On the positive side, associations keep neighborhoods looking sharp, maintain amenities you would never fund alone, and give you a layer of protection against a neighbor's choices dragging down your value. For busy families and first-time buyers, the predictability can be a real comfort.

The flip side is cost and control. Dues are a permanent line item that can rise over time, special assessments can arrive unexpectedly, and the rules mean you do not have total freedom over your own property. Enforcement can also feel heavy-handed in some communities. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on you, which is why matching the neighborhood to your lifestyle matters as much as matching the house to your budget.

One honest way to decide is to picture your daily life in the neighborhood five years from now. If you value low-maintenance living, community amenities, and a tidy, predictable street, the dues may feel like money well spent. If you dream of a workshop in the yard, a boat in the driveway, or full freedom to paint the house any color you like, a lighter-touch neighborhood may suit you better. Neither answer is wrong, and there is no shortage of both kinds of homes across Central Indiana.
questions-to-ask
Questions to Ask Before You Buy
Before you write an offer on an HOA home, get clear answers to a short list of questions. A good buyer's agent will help you gather these and read between the lines of the answers.

• What are the dues, and how often do they rise? Ask for a few years of history if you can get it.
  • How healthy are the reserves? A well-funded reserve lowers your risk of a surprise assessment.
  • Are any special assessments planned? This is the question that saves buyers the most heartache.
  • What does the leasing policy allow? This is critical if you might rent the home someday.
  • Are there restrictions I would find frustrating? Fences, parking, and exterior changes top the list.

If you are new to the process, our first time home buyer guide for Indianapolis walks through how these steps fit into the bigger picture. When you work with a Your Realty Link agent, you do not have to chase this paperwork alone. As MIBOR members, our team knows how to request association documents and what the answers really mean, so you can buy with confidence rather than crossed fingers.
highlight: Never waive the chance to read the HOA's budget and reserves. The rulebook tells you how to live there, but the financials tell you whether a surprise assessment is waiting for you after you close.
Daniel Cope, Real Estate Broker, Your Realty Link
faqs: Are HOAs mandatory in Central Indiana suburbs?

In most newer subdivisions and planned communities, yes. When an HOA governs the neighborhood, membership and dues are automatic and not optional. Many older Indianapolis neighborhoods have no mandatory HOA, so it varies by community.
Can an HOA really tell me what to do with my own home?
Within the limits of its recorded covenants, yes. HOAs can regulate things like exterior paint, fences, parking, and rentals. That is why reading the CC and Rs before you close is so important.
What is an HOA special assessment?

It is an extra charge beyond regular dues, usually to fund a large repair or cover a shortfall. Reviewing the association's reserves and meeting minutes before buying helps you gauge how likely one is.

seo_title: Selling a House As-Is in Indiana | Your Realty Link
meta_desc: Selling a house as-is in Indiana does not erase your disclosure duty. Learn what as-is really means, how to price it, and how to sell to the right buyer.
hero_sub: As-is does not mean no disclosure and no inspection. Here is what selling as-is really involves in Indiana, and how to do it the right way.
schema_headline: Selling a House As-Is in Indiana
schema_desc: A plain-English guide to selling a home as-is in Indiana, including disclosure duties, inspections, pricing, and honest marketing.
intro: If life has handed you a house you need to sell without pouring money into repairs, you are not alone, and you have options. An as-is sale is a common and completely legitimate path in Indiana, whether you inherited a property, you are a landlord who is simply worn out, or the home needs more work than you can take on right now. But as-is is one of the most misunderstood terms in real estate. It does not mean what many sellers assume it means, and getting it wrong can cost you. Here is how it actually works in Indiana.
sections: what-as-is-means
What Selling As-Is Really Means in Indiana

Selling as-is is a straightforward promise to buyers: you will not be making repairs. You are offering the home in its current condition, and the buyer accepts that they are taking it that way. It signals up front that you are not planning to fix the roof, replace the furnace, or patch the things a buyer might otherwise ask you to address. For the right seller, that clarity is a genuine relief.

What as-is does not do is switch off every other part of a normal sale. It is not a magic phrase that removes your legal responsibilities or strips the buyer of their rights. In Indiana, two things in particular still apply no matter how loudly the listing says as-is: your duty to disclose what you know, and the buyer's right to inspect. Misunderstanding those two points is where as-is sellers get into trouble, so let us take them one at a time.

It also helps to say plainly what as-is is not. It is not a way to unload a home nobody wants, and it is not an admission that something is wrong. Plenty of solid, livable homes sell as-is every year in Central Indiana simply because the owner does not want the hassle of repairs. As-is is a strategy, and used correctly it can make your sale simpler, faster, and far less stressful.
disclosure-duty
As-Is Does Not Erase Your Disclosure Duty

Indiana law requires most residential sellers to complete a seller's disclosure form, and selling as-is does not exempt you from it. The disclosure asks you to report known material defects, the problems you are actually aware of with the roof, foundation, systems, water intrusion, and more. As-is tells the buyer you will not fix those things. It does not give you permission to hide them.

This distinction matters enormously. If you know the basement takes on water every spring, you disclose it, even in an as-is sale. What you cannot do is stay quiet about a defect you know exists just to get a cleaner sale. Honesty here is not only the law, it is also your protection. A well-documented disclosure, paired with an as-is listing, tells buyers exactly what they are getting and helps shield you from claims down the road.

If you are unsure what counts as a material defect or how to complete the form for an unusual situation, do not guess. Your agent can walk you through it, and for legal specifics it is always wise to confirm with an Indiana real estate attorney. When in doubt, disclose.
inspection
Buyers Can Still Inspect the Home

The second surprise for many as-is sellers is that buyers can still order a home inspection. Selling as-is does not remove the buyer's ability to hire an inspector and learn everything they can about the property before closing. What changes is the expectation of what happens next.

In a traditional sale, an inspection often leads to a repair request or a credit. In an as-is sale, the buyer inspects mostly for their own knowledge and peace of mind, understanding that you are not agreeing to fix what they find. They may still choose to walk away if the inspection reveals something they cannot live with, depending on how the contract is written. That is why pricing and honest marketing matter so much, which brings us to the next point.

Because of this, the smart move for an as-is seller is not to discourage inspections but to price and present the home so that what an inspector finds is roughly what the buyer already expected. When there are no ugly surprises, inspections tend to confirm the deal rather than derail it. Transparency up front is what keeps an as-is sale on track from offer to closing.
who-sells
Who Typically Sells As-Is

People choose as-is sales for all kinds of reasons, and many of them are stressful life moments rather than simple preferences. If you are in one of these situations, know that selling as-is is a normal, respectable way forward, not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

• Estate and inherited homes: heirs often live out of state or simply cannot take on repairs to a loved one's property.
  • Tired landlords: longtime rental owners who are ready to be done and do not want to renovate a worn unit.
  • Distressed situations: divorce, financial strain, or a move that has to happen quickly.
  • Homes needing major work: properties where the cost of repairs is more than the seller can or wants to spend.

If you are settling an estate, the process carries its own steps and emotions. Our guide to probate and estate home sales in Indianapolis covers that path in more detail. Whatever brought you here, the goal is the same: a clean, honest sale that lets you move on without unnecessary stress.
pricing
Pricing an As-Is Home Realistically

The most important decision in an as-is sale is the price, because price is how you attract the right buyer. An as-is home will generally not sell for the same figure as a comparable home that has been updated and is move-in ready. Buyers factor in the work they will have to do, and a realistic price reflects that from the start. Overpricing an as-is home is the fastest way to have it sit on the market and grow stale.

The right way to set that price is with a comparative market analysis, a careful look at what similar homes in similar condition have actually sold for in your area. This is far more reliable than an online estimate, which cannot see that your home needs a new roof or that the kitchen is original. Our post on what your home is worth in Indianapolis explains why a real analysis beats an automated guess.

Priced correctly, an as-is home can move efficiently, because you are speaking directly to buyers who want a project or an investment. Priced too high, it lingers, and a long time on the market often leads to a lower final number than if you had started realistically in the first place.
how-we-market
How Your Realty Link Sells an As-Is Home Honestly

Selling as-is well is really about matching your home to the buyers who want it. That means marketing the property honestly, describing its condition plainly, and reaching investors, flippers, and value-minded buyers who are looking for exactly this kind of opportunity. Trying to hide the condition only wastes everyone's time and leads to deals that fall apart late in the process.

At Your Realty Link, Principal Broker Janet Giles-Schultz and our team of MIBOR agents help Central Indiana sellers navigate as-is sales with honesty and care. We help you complete your disclosure accurately, price the home against real comparable sales, and present it to the right audience. highlight: As-is is a pricing and marketing strategy, not a way to skip disclosure. Tell buyers exactly what you know, price the home for its true condition, and the right buyer will come.

faqs: Does selling as-is mean I do not have to disclose problems in Indiana?
No. Indiana still requires most sellers to complete a seller's disclosure and report known material defects. As-is means you will not make repairs, not that you can hide known problems.
Can a buyer still get an inspection on an as-is home?
Yes. Buyers can still hire an inspector to learn about the property. The difference is that you are not agreeing to fix whatever the inspection finds.
Will I get less money selling as-is?

Often an as-is home sells for less than a comparable updated home, because buyers account for the work needed. Pricing it realistically with a market analysis helps you attract serious buyers and avoid a long time on the market.

intro: You are days from owning your new home, and there is one last step many Central Indiana buyers underestimate: the final walk-through. This is the short visit, usually a day or two before closing, where you confirm the home is in the condition you agreed to buy. It is not a formality to rush through on your way to the closing table. Done well, it catches problems while you still have leverage to fix them. Done carelessly, it can leave you discovering issues after the home is legally yours. Here is how to do it right.
sections: what-it-is
What the Final Walk-Through Is (and Is Not)

The single most important thing to understand is that the final walk-through is a confirmation, not a re-inspection. You are not there to renegotiate the deal or to evaluate the home as if you were seeing it for the first time. That work already happened earlier during your home inspection. The walk-through simply verifies that the home is in the same shape it was when you agreed to buy it, and that any promised repairs are done.

Think of it as answering three questions. Is the home in the condition I expected? Were the agreed-upon repairs completed? Did anything change since I last saw it? If the answer to all three is yes, you head to closing with confidence. If something is off, the walk-through is your chance to raise it before the sale is final, while you still have room to ask for a solution.

Because it is a confirmation rather than a fresh evaluation, the walk-through usually goes quickly when everything is in order. That is exactly the goal. But quick should never mean careless. The handful of minutes you spend testing systems and checking repairs is your final safeguard, and it is far easier to resolve an issue now than after the deed is in your name.
when-happens
When the Walk-Through Happens

In most Central Indiana transactions, the final walk-through takes place shortly before closing, often the day before or the morning of. The timing is deliberate. You want it close enough to closing that the home's condition is unlikely to change afterward, but with enough breathing room that if you spot a problem, there is still time to address it before you sign.

Your agent will schedule and attend it with you. Give yourself enough time to be thorough rather than squeezing it into a few rushed minutes. Bring your paperwork, including the inspection report and any repair agreements, so you can check promised items against what you actually see. A little patience here protects one of the biggest purchases of your life.

It also helps to know who will not be there. In most cases the sellers have already moved out or are in the process, so the home may be empty, which actually makes it easier to spot damage and confirm what conveys. If the sellers are still occupying the home, note anything that could be affected by their final move-out and plan to confirm it is resolved before you close.
checklist
Your Central Indiana Final Walk-Through Checklist
Walk the home methodically, room by room, and do not assume anything works just because it looks fine. Turn things on. Open and close things. Here is a practical checklist to guide you.

• Agreed repairs are done: confirm every repair from your negotiation was completed, and ask for receipts if professional work was required.
  • Systems work: test the heating and cooling, run faucets and showers, flush toilets, and check for hot water.
  • Appliances that convey: make sure the refrigerator, range, dishwasher, and any other included appliances are present and running.
  • Nothing was removed: confirm items meant to stay, like light fixtures, blinds, or a mounted television bracket, are still there.
  • No new damage: look for scrapes, holes, or damage from the sellers moving out.
  • Broom-clean condition: the home should be reasonably clean and empty of the sellers' belongings and trash.
  • Utilities are on: lights, outlets, and major systems should be powered so you can actually test them.
  • Windows and doors: open and lock them, and check that all keys, openers, and codes will be provided.

Pay special attention to areas that were hidden on your earlier visits. Look under sinks for leaks, check the spots where furniture used to sit for stains or damage, test the garage door opener, and peek at the water heater and furnace. Sellers moving out can reveal, or occasionally cause, issues that were not visible when the home was staged and full of belongings. A slow drip behind a washing machine or a gouge in the floor under a rug is exactly the kind of thing this visit exists to catch.
something-wrong
What to Do If Something Is Not Right

If your walk-through turns up a problem, do not panic and do not simply proceed hoping it works out. Tell your agent right away. Because you have not closed yet, you still have options, and the right one depends on what you find and what your contract says. Your remaining contingency protections and the specifics of your purchase agreement shape what you can ask for.

• Ask the seller to fix it: for a promised repair that was not done, the seller can be asked to complete it before closing.
  • Negotiate a credit: the parties may agree to a closing credit so you can handle the issue yourself.
  • Delay the closing: if the problem is significant, closing can sometimes be postponed until it is resolved.
  • Use an escrow holdback: money can be set aside at closing to cover a repair that cannot be finished in time.

None of these should be handled on your own in the moment. This is exactly where an experienced agent earns their keep, negotiating calmly and protecting your position. The worst outcome is staying silent, closing anyway, and then owning a problem you could have solved a day earlier.
leads-to-closing
How the Walk-Through Leads Into Closing Day

When the walk-through checks out, you are cleared for the final step. Closing day is when ownership officially transfers, you sign your paperwork, and the keys become yours. A clean walk-through means you arrive at the table without last-minute surprises, which is exactly how it should feel. If you want to understand the money side of that day, our post on closing costs in Indiana is a helpful companion, and it pairs well with our first time home buyer guide for Indianapolis.

At Your Realty Link, Principal Broker Janet Giles-Schultz and our MIBOR team guide buyers through every one of these steps, from offer to inspection to that final walk-through and across the closing table. The walk-through is a small window with big consequences, and having a professional beside you means nothing important slips through. When it is done right, you unlock the door to your new home with total confidence.

One last piece of advice: keep your walk-through notes until after closing. If you agreed to a credit, a holdback, or a last-minute repair, having a clear record of what you observed and what was promised makes the closing table smoother. Small details, documented, prevent big misunderstandings.
highlight: Treat the walk-through as your last checkpoint, not a lap of honor. Turn on every system, confirm every promised repair, and speak up before you sign, because your leverage disappears the moment you close.
Daniel Cope, Real Estate Broker, Your Realty Link
faqs: Is the final walk-through the same as a home inspection?
No. The inspection earlier in the process evaluates the home's condition in depth. The walk-through simply confirms the home is in the agreed condition and that promised repairs were completed.
What happens if I find a problem during the walk-through?

Tell your agent immediately, since you have not closed yet. Options can include asking the seller to fix it, negotiating a credit, delaying closing, or setting up an escrow holdback, depending on your contract.
When does the final walk-through happen in Indiana?
It usually takes place shortly before closing, often the day before or the morning of, so the home's condition is confirmed as close to closing as possible.
